strengths: Clean data-centric theoretical framework starting from triplet distribution rather than assuming BT holds; CPRD is a natural object to study independent of generative assumptions
Elegant characterization of BT representability through positive-negative conditional independence (Theorem 4.4) providing both necessary and sufficient conditions
Novel insight that BT learning performs KL projection at preference level (Theorem 5.2), clarifying what is recovered under model misspecification
Unified sample complexity analysis across settings (tabular, linear, neural networks) with clear identification of margin and connectivity as fundamental governing factors
Well-organized presentation with logical progression from definitions to characterization to learning analysis
weaknesses: Major practical gap: authors acknowledge that margin cannot be easily evaluated in practice (implicit target score), connectivity optimization strategies are unknown, and assumption that target function is known during data collection is unrealistic

Positive-negative conditional independence assumption is strong and likely violated in real preference data; no guidance on verification, failure modes, or severity of violations; intransitivity in real data not addressed

Purely synthetic experiments at small scale (m=16, d=128); no real preference datasets, no comparisons with other reward modeling methods, no evidence framework improves real systems; experiments mainly validate theory rather than demonstrating utility

Sample complexity bounds potentially suboptimal: depend on 1/λ_conn via worst-case minimization, no lower bounds provided to assess tightness, Rademacher complexity for neural networks can be prohibitively large; bounded hypothesis class assumption may not hold

Limited technical novelty: CPRD is classical choice probability from decision theory, positive-negative conditional independence not new, BT characterization is clean presentation of existing ideas, connection to NCE underdeveloped; overall framework incremental over classical preference learning theory

Connectivity degree definition complex and difficult to compute/optimize in practice; Figure 2 shows non-monotonic relationship limiting actionability; no efficient algorithms provided for neural networks (requires solving optimization problem in Eq. 159)

Missing connection to LLM alignment applications where motivation originates; no discussion of how margin/connectivity relate to reward hacking or downstream performance; recent work on Direct Preference Optimization not adequately engaged
Agnostic misspecification case relegated to appendix despite practical relevance; no ablations or sensitivity analyses; generalization of results to other architectures unclear

strengths: Clean data-centric framework through CPRD that avoids presupposing BT model; intellectually principled starting point
Technically sound theoretical contributions with rigorous proofs; characterization of BT representability via conditional independence is precise and non-obvious
Comprehensive treatment unifying representability, learning objectives, and sample complexity into coherent framework
Identification of margin and connectivity as governing factors is useful and admits interpretable forms in special cases (Fiedler value, eigenvalues)
Strong experimental validation with well-designed synthetic experiments isolating predicted effects; real-world experiments show correlation with theory
Well-written paper with clear presentation, good motivation, and appropriate acknowledgment of limitations
Solid connection to related work (NCE, prior BT theory, graph-theoretic quantities)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: reinterprets well-studied BT model through data-centric lens; conditional independence assumption and KL projection are conceptually natural rather than surprising discoveries

Significant theory-practice gap: margin is difficult to optimize in practice since target score function is implicit; connectivity computation requires expensive minimax optimization; actionable strategies for improvement remain open

Restrictive assumptions: positive-negative conditional independence violated when negatives are edited or curated; sample complexity analysis assumes target score known when designing distributions—unrealistic since target is what we want to learn

Connectivity definition complex with poor practitioner intuition; computation stability issues (up to 95% relative std. deviation); requires specialized analysis per model class to connect to interpretable quantities

Limited real-world validation: only tests linear reward heads on frozen embeddings with 10K pairs; no downstream task performance evaluation; no experiments demonstrating practical utility of insights for improving data collection
Sample complexity bounds lack tightness analysis; no lower bounds or instance-specific optimality results; dependencies on 1/λ_conn appear but necessity unclear

Misspecification analysis underdeveloped: synthetic non-BT CPRD experiment somewhat artificial; real data misspecification patterns may differ; limited guidance on practitioner response to suspected misspecification

Experimental scope: synthetic experiments use small settings (m=16, d=128); real-world results show margin and connectivity can trade off (Table 2), deserving deeper analysis; missing comparisons with other modern preference learning frameworks
Incomplete treatment of conditional independence testing: noted as difficult in high dimensions but alternative diagnostics not explored in depth
Missing actionable guidance on typical connectivity values, how to improve connectivity in practice, or how to extend theory beyond BT models
